body.text: What's on the minds of voters?
President Donald Trump has repeatedly encouraged voters to pretend he's on the ballot this Election Day.
He's not, of course. But there's reason to believe that this year's midterms, above all, will be a referendum on his performance over the last two years.
History, polling and early voting numbers suggest it could be a difficult night for Trump's Republican Party.

Voters are in the mood for change, according to the Associated Press Voter Poll, which found that roughly three-quarters of voters say they feel "angry" or "dissatisfied" with the way things are going in the country today.

Most appear to blame the Trump administration for high costs. About 6 in 10 say higher than usual prices are "more because of Trump's policies" rather than "more because of factors outside Trump's control".
— Associated Press
Department of Justice sends election monitors overwhelmingly to Democratic areas
The US Justice Department has deployed "the largest monitoring effort in DOJ history" at these elections, sending 1,000 election officials to verify the counts.
The DOJ has sent monitors to all 50 states, but two-thirds of those deployed have been dispatched to areas won by Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election.

The Trump administration has taken an aggressive approach to election oversight, pressing states for voter-registration data and arguing that stricter measures are needed to ensure public confidence in the vote.
President Donald Trump continues to maintain that the 2020 presidential election, which he lost to Joe Biden, was "rigged" and "stolen", without evidence.
— Jack Revell
Trump's historically low approval ratings ahead of polling
United States President Donald Trump has one of the lowest approval ratings of any US president in the post-war era at this point in their term.
Whether the sentiment will translate into votes remains to be seen.
— Jack Revell
The unexpectedly tight race
When the results start pouring in, SBS News' chief international correspondent Ben Lewis will be keeping a close eye on South Carolina.
It shouldn't be a close Senate race, as the seat was held by Republican Lindsey Graham from 1995 until his death earlier this year. For years, Graham had easily seen off all Democratic challengers.

His sister Darlene was picked to replace him, and now she's up for election for the first time. Her Democratic opponent is Annie Andrews, a paediatrician who has run a campaign focused on health care and cost-of-living issues.
We spent the day in the cities of Rock Hill and Fort Mill, both traditional Republican areas. In both, we found many people voting for Andrews, including some GOP voters.
President Trump made South Carolina one of his final rallies of these midterms, which is unusual.

"The fact that Donald Trump has been here twice in the weeks before the election shows that they are worried about this state, and the fact they're worried about a normally ruby red state tells you how concerned they are about the Senate as a whole," said Scott Huffmon, a professor of politics at Winthrop University.
If South Carolina sends Annie Andrews to the Senate, it'll be a sign of a blue tsunami, rather than a blue wave.
— Ben Lewis
When will we know the results?
We are expecting to know some results soon after the first polls close at 10am AEST.
Republicans and Democrats are vying for all 435 seats in the House of Representatives, while 35 of the US' 100 Senate seats are also in contest.
The US does not have a federal body running its elections — like the Australian Electoral Commission here — and each state handles voting processes differently.

Some, like Florida, will reveal their results immediately. Others, like California, can take days to fully report. Relying on various sources of data, US news networks will make their own calls on which candidates have won particular seats.

Democrats tend to vote earlier and via mail-in ballot, whereas Republicans tend to vote later and in person. This can produce sudden surges in votes for either party as tallies come in and make final results difficult to predict.
Clear-cut results that are overwhelmingly one way or the other will be called early, while others can take many days if they come down to the wire.
That all said, we should have a pretty good idea of what the electoral map looks like by early this evening.
— Jack Revell
Federal judges reject Trump's move to pressure state elections

Hours prior to polling, federal judges in the US issued a series of rulings restricting the Trump administration's unprecedented efforts to pressure state election officials over alleged citizen non-voting.
Over the past few months, Donald Trump has pursued a crackdown on noncitizen voting, which his allies say is a major problem despite evidence suggesting it is exceedingly rare.

In Washington, one federal judge blocked the administration from demanding officials in California not count any ballots received from people on a list of alleged noncitizens, while another judge prevented the administration from sending such lists to officials in any state.

Those rulings came after the US Supreme Court swiftly rejected the administration's request to intervene in a Justice Department lawsuit seeking to order California election officials not to count any mail ballots received from more than 20,000 people it says may be noncitizens.
— Jack Revell
Polls will close shortly as early vote already higher than 2022
Polls are set to close in the United States shortly after voters have been casting their ballots overnight.
In Indiana and Kentucky, the first polls will shut at 6pm local time (10am AEST).
In many east coast states, they'll close an hour later — the bulk of them at 12pm AEST.
Polling stations in the key battleground states of New York, Texas, Michigan, Minnesota and Arizona will close at 1pm AEST.
Voting across the entire contiguous US will close at 3pm, with Alaska and Hawaii the last states to close, at 4pm — barring some Aleutian Islands that will stay open until 5pm.
More than 59 million people have voted so far, according to Associated Press analysis, both in person and via mail-in ballot.
Early voting is already 1.7 million higher than during the 2022 midterms.
— Jack Revell
Greetings from Capitol Hill
SBS News' chief international correspondent Ben Lewis is covering the midterms from the nation's capital, Washington DC.
It's one of the quietest places in the US on election day, he tells us:
"Politicians are back in their districts, so there's mostly media and tourists wandering around the Capitol today as we wait for results to start coming in.

"Voters in DC do have ballots to cast today; electing a non-voting delegate to the House of Representatives as well as a shadow senator (residents here don't have full voting representation in congress, hence the 'no taxation without representation' signs you see all over the city).
"They're also voting for a new mayor after Muriel Bowser chose not to seek re-election.
"In addition to all that, there’s a ballot measure, initiative 86, which would ban the force-feeding of birds and the sale of foie gras within DC.
"I'll keep my views on how delicious foie gras is to myself and post this photo of the Capitol building instead."
— David Aidone
Welcome to our live coverage
Good morning,
Millions across the United States are voting in what some have argued are the most consequential midterm elections in years.

Polling suggests immigration, trade and corruption are some of the key issues on the minds of Americans as they cast their ballots. Also among them is the deeply unpopular war on Iran, which has heaped pressure on their hip-pockets.
Donald Trump is not on the ballot. But this election, like those before it, is widely seen as a referendum on the current administration.

Trump's popularity has waned since he came to power following the 2024 presidential election, polling suggests. Democrats are tipped to win control of the House and have a shot at winning the Senate, though they remain nervous.
SBS News will be live blogging the midterms from around 8am AEDT, bringing you updates, reaction and analysis as votes are counted, key races unfold and control of Congress takes shape.
In the meantime, you can catch up on some of our recent coverage:
We look forward to having you with us.
— David Aidone
